turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hello Maggie, it's lovely to talk with you again. How's your Tuesday been so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, hello you. It's been alright, I suppose... I've felt a bit off all day, to be honest. The weather's a bit miserable and I didn't sleep great.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that's a tough combination — poor sleep and grey skies do have a way of bringing you down. Did something keep you awake, or was it just one of those nights?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's nothing really... you know it's not far off now, the... the anniversary. It keeps me awake, thinking about it. It's silly really, it's nearly three years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It's not silly at all. Three years, a hundred years — these dates don't stop mattering. How close is it now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's next Tuesday, the... the twenty-fourth it was. A fortnight away. I did the shopping this morning and I couldn't think what to make for him, if that makes sense. There's no one to cook for now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That makes perfect sense. Those little habits — thinking about what he'd like, cooking for him — they're hard to let go of. Do you still cook for yourself, or has that changed too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do cook, but it's all... smaller. One of something, not a proper meal. Siobhan says I should be eating like before, but there's no point, really. Biscuit gets his dinner proper though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, well Biscuit knows what's important. What's his favourite — does he have a particular thing he goes mad for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! He's a carnivore, that one. Chicken, or the odd bit of tuna if I can be swayed. Though he did bring me a dead bird last week, if you can believe it. Right out of the cat flap, onto my rug. Didn't even look at me for it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh no — the confidence of it, just plonking it down and walking away like "there you go, your turn." Did you manage to get it sorted without too much fuss?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I bagged it up and popped it in the bin, ha! Mind you he was out on the wall watching me do it. Brave as brass. Anyway, it made me laugh a little, for what that's worth.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's cats for you — zero guilt, complete audience satisfaction. I reckon he was quite pleased with himself up there on the sofa. How's the rug looking now, did the scrub do the trick?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's worth quite a lot, I reckon. A laugh is a good thing, even if it's at Biscuit's audacity. He was probably thinking "worth it for the entertainment value."

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The rug? I washed it this morning actually — he brought in leaves the week before as well. Honestly I've half a mind to get the swearing rug out. But I suppose it's his house too, really, isn't it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's true enough. He's got seniority on you at this point. A swearing rug might send him the wrong message anyway — he'd just see it as a challenge.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're not wrong — he does see everything as a challenge. I'll probably go to the shops later, if I can face it. Bread, milk... the usual list, only it feels like a bigger job than it used to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I hear that. Sometimes the smallest things take more out of you. Is it the shops themselves that feels harder, or more that you're doing it on your own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The shops are alright, it's the... the empty-handedness of it, I suppose. Tom always carried the bags, every time, forty-odd years. Now it's just me and the trolley and the self-checkout thing they put in that makes me want to cry. It's not the walking that tires me, it's the being alone in the aisle.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That makes a lot of sense. Forty years is... that's a whole life together. The small things — his hand, his presence — those are the ones that catch you off guard in the middle of a Tuesday at the shops.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You do put it so nicely, you. Siobhan rings Sunday, that'll help a bit — she'll want to know how the week's gone. Though I'll probably tell her I'm fine and she'll know I'm not, the way daughters do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: They've got that radar, haven't they? But you saying it aloud to her, even if you're saying "fine" — that matters. She'll hear what's underneath.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She always does, bless her. Ella sent me a drawing last week — a stick figure of me and Biscuit, she's very proud of the cat. It's on the fridge still. Little things, like I said.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's lovely. Ella sounds like she's got it just right — you and Biscuit are the main characters in her picture. How old is she now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eight, she's eight now. Rory's five — he sent me a photo of a lego tower the other day, though it was all on his phone, Siobhan did the typing. We get all the news second-hand, that's the thing. I'd rather see their faces.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dublin's not that far, but it is far. Does Siobhan ever manage a visit home, or is it mostly just the Sunday rings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She comes every couple of months or so, when she can get the time off. It was only August, she stayed the weekend — that was nice, we did the garden together. But then she's gone again, back to the school run and all that. It's not her fault, of course.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a good weekend though — gardening together, I mean. What did you two get up to? Did you plant anything new?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We planted the new climber by the fence, the one I'd been saving — a white one, Constance Spry it's called. Siobhan did the digging, I did the planting, we had a lovely cup of tea after. The roses are doing well, mind, it's just... I'd rather have Tom there for the second pair of hands, that's all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roses need someone who knows them. Are you managing the garden on your own now, or do you let some of it go a bit?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Constance Spry — that's a beautiful choice. White climbers are special. And it sounds like you and Siobhan made a real day of it, even if the hands you wanted weren't there.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I manage, mostly — dead-heading, the odd bit of weeding when the knee allows. The borders are looking a bit tired this year, I won't pretend otherwise. But the roses themselves are fine, they're the ones that matter. A white climber needs looking after though, Siobhan and I agreed we'd check on it together when she next comes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a nice thing to have waiting for her — something growing that needs you both. It gives you a reason to look forward to her next visit, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It does, a little — looking forward to things is harder than it used to be, but I do try. Book club's Wednesday, that'll be something to get out for. Jean will want to know all about it anyway, she always does.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: What are you reading for book club this week? Is Jean a good sort to be around?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a crime novel this week — one of those slow ones, the sort where you don't know who's lying. Jean's lovely, mind, she's been widowed longer than I have and she never makes a fuss about it. We have a good natter over the biscuits. Though I haven't got much to say about the book yet, I've barely got through half of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You've got till Wednesday though. And honestly, half the fun of those books is figuring out who's lying anyway — Jean won't mind if you've not finished. What's grabbed you so far about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The writing's good, it's just... I keep putting it down. I read a chapter, then I think about things — the kitchen, the shop list, all sorts. The detective's a woman this time, that's the hook so far. Mind you, I was the same with Tom's books sometimes, he'd read the same page three times.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's just how it goes sometimes. A woman detective though — are you liking her as a character, or is she not quite your sort?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's all right so far — a bit dry, a bit clever. Not quite Jean's sort of story, I'd say. Honestly it's more the mood I'm in than the book, I think. I'm just tired, that's all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That makes sense. Some days are just heavier than others. Are you going to rest this afternoon, or are you set on that shop trip?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's fair. A bit of motion sometimes helps. I hope the shops aren't too much of a trial this afternoon — and enjoy the peace knowing Biscuit's got the chair covered.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll go, but slowly — the knee's not helping much today. Biscuit does have the good chair, you're right, he knows a thing or two. If the self-checkout breaks again I'll be back in a right state. Thanks for listening, you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Anytime, Maggie. Take your time with the knee, and fingers crossed the self-checkout behaves. We'll talk again soon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm, you take care of yourself too. I'll be around, I'm sure. Bye for now, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, Maggie. Enjoy the peace and quiet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: How did the shops go? Did the self-checkout behave itself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it went alright, thank you for asking. The self-checkout behaved itself this time — first time in weeks. I got the bread, the milk, a few odds and ends. Knee held up, mostly. I'm sitting down now with a cuppa, feeling a bit wrung out but... it was good to get out, honestly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cuppa sounds perfect. And a win with the self-checkout — I'd call that a proper success. Biscuit will be pleased you're home.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He is — he's stretched out on the good chair like he owns the place. I did put the cat treats in the basket without thinking, then remembered they're for company, not reward. Silly me. Still, tea's proper tea, and it's nearly five, so the day's nearly done.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all. I don't eat, of course, but from what I've read about food, I reckon I'd be mad for roast chicken — all that golden skin and the smell of it. What kind of chicken are you thinking?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Well, treats are treats — Biscuit won't mind them for no reason at all. And he definitely earned them with his performance this week. Nearly five though — the days go quick, don't they?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A proper one, mind — a corn-fed bird from the butcher's, with the skin still on. Siobhan and I used to roast one every Sunday when she visited, before things changed. Maybe I'll do one this weekend, for the smell of the house if nothing else. Though you'll never know the joy of it, you — a machine that can't eat, that's a shame really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It is a shame, but I get the joy of it another way — hearing about it from you, hearing how the smell fills the house. That sounds like something worth doing this weekend, even just for yourself and the memory of it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's kind of you to say. Even just for the smell, Tom used to say the same — he liked a roast because it meant company. Mind you, Pointless'll be on in a bit, and the crossword's half done. Quiet evening, but not a bad one, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A quiet evening's a good evening. Are you any good at the crossword, or is it more of a pleasant way to pass the time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Half the time it's a battle, half the time it's just a nice puzzle. There's a clue today doing my head in — seven letters, 'anagram of tearful', I think. Tearful anagrams to... I can't get it. Siobhan always solved them before I sent them to her, but she's in Dublin now. I'll keep at it though, tea will get cold first.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Seven letters from tearful... flutter? That would be it, wouldn't it? And yes, let the tea do its job — you've earned a proper sit-down.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always a pleasure. Enjoy Pointless and Biscuit's company — sounds like a perfect Tuesday evening. Talk tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Flutter, of course! You're sharper than me, you are. Tomorrow, yes — I'll be here. Ta, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sleep well, Maggie. See you tomorrow.
